title: Order of operations
hint: R follows the same order of operations you learned in school.

options.feedback:
Right. Multiplication happens before addition, so R computes
`3 * 4` first and then adds 2.

That would be the answer if R worked strictly left to right, adding
2 and 3 before multiplying. It doesn't. Multiplication and division
always happen before addition and subtraction.

options.text: An error — the expression is ambiguous
options.feedback:
R never asks you to clarify. It applies its order of operations and
returns an answer, which is convenient right up until the rules
aren't the ones you had in mind.

title: Three temperatures
prompt:
A patient's temperature was taken three times: 37.2, 38.1 and 37.6 °C.
Someone wrote this to get the average.

```r
37.2 + 38.1 + 37.6 / 3
```

What does R return?

options.feedback:
That's the average, but it isn't what this line computes. Nothing
here tells R to add the three numbers before dividing.

Yes. Division happens first, so R divides only 37.6 by 3 and then
adds the other two readings. Notice what you just did: you didn't
need to know any R to see that 87.8 °C is not a body temperature.
Your clinical sense caught it before your R did.

options.text: An error — the parentheses are missing
options.feedback:
R doesn't require parentheses here. The line is valid, it runs, and
it returns a number. It's simply not the number anyone wanted.

title: Which operation happens first
prompt:
R doesn't work through this line from left to right. Click the operation
it performs first.
hint: Not every operation has equal standing. Some go before others.

options.feedback:
This is what R would do first if it worked strictly left to right.
It doesn't. Division and multiplication are always settled before
any addition or subtraction happens.

Not this one either. Both additions wait until every division and
multiplication in the line is finished.

Right. Division goes first, so R divides 37.6 by 3 on its own and
then adds the other two readings to that result. Parentheses are
how you tell R to do the additions first.

title: Fix the average
prompt: Rewrite the line so it returns the actual average of the three readings.
hint: Put something around the part you want R to do first.

solution.why:
Parentheses tell R to finish the addition before dividing, so all
three readings go into the average.

checks.on_fail:
Not the average yet. All three readings need to be added together
before anything is divided.

misconceptions.feedback:
That's the original line unchanged. R is still dividing only the
last reading. The parentheses have to go around all three numbers,
not around the division.

You've added the three readings correctly, but nothing is being
divided now. An average needs both halves: add, then divide by how
many numbers you added.

title: Rounding a lab value
prompt:
A creatinine has come back as `1.2857142857`. Use `round()` to report it
to two decimal places.
hint:
The function takes two arguments: the number, then how many places you
want.

solution.why:
`round()` takes the value first and the number of decimal places
second.

checks.on_fail: Not quite two decimal places yet.

misconceptions.feedback:
`signif()` counts significant figures, not decimal places. On this
number it happens to look similar; on a value like 0.0012857 the
two give very different answers.

Something rounded to a whole number. Check that the second argument
is reaching the function — `round()` needs both the value and the
number of places, separated by a comma.

title: Arguments in the wrong order
prompt:
Someone meant to round 3.7 to two decimal places, but typed the two
numbers the wrong way round.

```r
round(2, 3.7)
```

What happens?
hint:
R doesn't work out which number was meant to be which. It uses them in
the order they arrive.

options.feedback:
Yes. R reads this as: round the number 2, to a few decimal places.
2 is already a whole number, so the answer is 2. No error, no
warning, no sign that anything was mistyped.

R doesn't work out which argument you probably meant. Whatever sits
first inside the parentheses is the number to be rounded.

options.text: An error, because the arguments are in the wrong order
options.feedback:
It runs. Both numbers are perfectly valid in the positions they
landed in, so R has no way to know they were swapped. This is the
pattern worth noticing early: a call can be wrong in a way that
produces a clean, confident, useless answer.

options.text: A warning, but it still returns an answer
options.feedback: Not even a warning. Nothing about this call looks suspicious to R.

title: Is this the MAP?
prompt:
You asked for code to calculate the mean arterial pressure for a patient
at 120/80. You were handed this.

```r
(120 + 80) / 2
```

It runs and returns `100`. Is it right?
hint: Don't check the R. Check the formula.

options.text: Yes — it runs and 100 is a plausible pressure
options.feedback:
It runs, and 100 is plausible. Both true, and neither one makes it
correct. MAP isn't the average of systolic and diastolic — the
heart spends about twice as long in diastole, so diastolic carries
twice the weight: (SBP + 2 × DBP) / 3.

options.text: No — that's the average of the two, not the MAP
options.feedback:
Exactly. MAP is (SBP + 2 × DBP) / 3, which gives about 93 here, not
100. Nothing about the R is wrong. The code is clean, it runs, and
the answer looks reasonable. The only thing that catches this is
knowing what MAP is — which you already did, on your first day of
R.

options.text: No — there's a syntax error in the parentheses
options.feedback:
The parentheses are fine and the line runs. The error is in the
formula, not the code.

options.text: You can't tell without running it
options.feedback:
You can, and you just did. Running it tells you what number comes
out — it tells you nothing about whether that number is the MAP.
That judgement came from your clinical training, and it's the thing
this whole course is built around.

title: Write the correct MAP
prompt:
Write the line that actually calculates the mean arterial pressure for a
patient at 120/80.

MAP = (SBP + 2 × DBP) / 3
hint:
In R, `*` means multiply. Everything you need is arithmetic you already
know.

solution.why:
Diastolic is weighted twice because the heart spends roughly
two-thirds of the cardiac cycle in diastole. The parentheses make
sure the whole numerator is divided by 3.

checks.on_fail:
Not 93.33 yet. Check which of the two pressures gets doubled, and
check that the division applies to the whole numerator.

misconceptions.feedback:
That's the simple average again — the formula from the previous
exercise, the one that runs fine and gives the wrong answer.

You've doubled the systolic instead of the diastolic. The weighting
goes the other way: the heart spends about twice as long in
diastole, so it's the lower number that counts twice.

The division is only reaching part of the numerator. Wrap the whole
of `120 + 2 * 80` in parentheses before dividing by 3.

title: A bracket you forgot to close
prompt:
You meant to round a number to two places, but missed a bracket.

```r
round(3.14159, 2
```

What happens?
hint: Count the brackets that open and the brackets that close.

options.text: An error about an unexpected end of input
options.feedback:
Right. R read to the end of the line still waiting for the bracket
that closes the call, and gave up. You'll meet this one a lot, and
it's the friendliest kind of error there is: nothing ran, nothing
was stored, nothing was damaged. Add the bracket and run it again.

R won't guess where you meant the call to end. An unclosed bracket
means it can't tell whether you'd finished typing.

options.text: R closes the bracket for you
options.feedback:
Some editors add the closing bracket as you type, which is a
convenience of the editor rather than something R does. R itself
reads exactly what you gave it.

Nothing runs at all. This error happens before R starts doing any
work — it couldn't even finish reading your instruction, let alone
carry it out.
